rounds.reviewStatus: Practice guidelines; also reviewed by an expert panel

clues.title: Sequence consequence
clues.text: Three DNA bases are deleted. Phenylalanine 508 is lost, but the reading frame stays intact.

clues.title: Functional evidence
clues.text: Experiments reported in the record show impaired CFTR function. An in-frame deletion can still damage a protein.

clues.title: Clinical evidence
clues.text: This is the well-studied F508del allele, repeatedly observed in people with cystic fibrosis and supported by expert review.

rounds.explanation: Keeping the reading frame does not guarantee a working channel. Experimental and clinical evidence support this disease-causing allele. Cystic fibrosis is recessive: the genotype matters, and one copy alone does not establish the diagnosis.

rounds.context: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition

clues.title: Sequence consequence
clues.text: Two bases are deleted near the start of BRCA1. The deletion shifts the reading frame.

clues.title: Protein consequence
clues.text: The shifted frame introduces an early stop. A shortened or absent protein fits the established loss-of-function disease mechanism.

clues.title: Clinical evidence
clues.text: Also called 185delAG, this founder allele has been reported in many families with inherited cancer predisposition. An expert panel has assessed it.

rounds.explanation: The early frameshift and extensive clinical evidence support pathogenicity. Here that means increased inherited cancer risk, not certainty that a carrier will develop cancer.

rounds.reviewStatus: Criteria provided, multiple submitters, no conflicts

clues.title: Sequence consequence
clues.text: A single base substitution replaces glutamate with valine. The protein keeps its length.

clues.title: Functional evidence
clues.text: The altered haemoglobin can form fibres when deoxygenated, changing red-cell behaviour. A missense change can have a major effect.

clues.title: Clinical evidence
clues.text: This is HbS, also called Glu6Val in older numbering. Disease is associated with two HbS copies or HbS paired with certain other HBB alleles.

rounds.explanation: This well-established allele causes sickle cell disease in relevant two-allele combinations. A single copy usually produces sickle cell trait. Protein length and population frequency alone cannot settle pathogenicity.

clues.title: Sequence consequence
clues.text: Tyrosine is replaced with cysteine. A changed amino acid is a clue, not a verdict.

clues.title: Evidence in context
clues.text: The record discusses inconsistent computational predictions and observations alongside other BRCA variants. Finding a change in a cancer patient does not establish causation.

clues.title: Combined evidence
clues.text: An expert panel's multifactorial analysis places this variant in IARC class 1, the category used for changes not considered disease-causing.

rounds.explanation: The expert-panel classification is benign despite the missense consequence and some concerning experimental reports. The combined evidence carries more weight than the appearance of the sequence change alone.

clues.title: Sequence consequence
clues.text: The DNA spelling changes, but codon 85 still specifies glycine. The equals sign denotes an unchanged amino acid.

clues.title: Limits of this clue
clues.text: This is a synonymous variant. Such changes can sometimes affect RNA processing, so the protein notation alone cannot establish a classification.

clues.title: Record assessment
clues.text: The record has one criteria-based submission favouring a non-disease-causing interpretation. Its level of confidence falls short of a definitive benign assertion.

rounds.explanation: ClinVar records this variant as likely benign. The game groups benign and likely benign together while retaining the exact label and single-submitter review status. A synonymous change is not automatically benign.

rounds.reviewStatus: Criteria provided, multiple submitters, no conflicts

clues.title: Sequence consequence
clues.text: A DNA substitution leaves threonine 1299 unchanged. This is another synonymous variant.

clues.title: Supporting observations
clues.text: The wider variant record describes this change in control populations and in affected people carrying other disease-causing CFTR changes.

clues.title: Condition matters
clues.text: For cystic fibrosis specifically, multiple criteria-based submissions agree on the non-disease-causing side. The broader variant record includes uncertainty for a different condition.

rounds.explanation: For this cystic-fibrosis record, the classification is benign/likely benign. Its overall variant page has conflicting classifications across conditions. Always check which condition and record a verdict describes.

rounds.scope: Variant–condition record: hereditary breast ovarian cancer syndrome

clues.title: Sequence consequence
clues.text: Alanine is replaced by glycine. Both are small, neutral amino acids; this does not establish the effect on DNA repair.

clues.title: Population evidence
clues.text: Submissions report no population-database frequency and no published affected individuals. Absence from a database is not proof of harm.

clues.title: Evidence gap
clues.text: Computational modelling suggests little functional impact, but a prediction cannot settle the classification. The submission says the evidence is insufficient to resolve the disease association.

rounds.explanation: The evidence supports a variant of uncertain significance, not a finding of disease causation or safety. Predictions and rarity are insufficient to resolve this case.

clues.title: Sequence consequence
clues.text: Phenylalanine 508 is replaced with cysteine. This is not the F508del deletion, even though it affects the same amino-acid position.

clues.title: Interpretation
clues.text: A familiar position does not transfer the classification of a different allele. The exact DNA change and its supporting evidence matter.

clues.title: Submitter agreement
clues.text: The cystic-fibrosis record contains differing criteria-based interpretations, including benign assertions. ClinVar reports disagreement rather than a single settled classification.

rounds.explanation: Conflicting classifications are different from a consensus VUS, but both belong in this game's uncertain/conflicting bucket. The correct response is to recognise the disagreement, not to take a majority vote or copy F508del's verdict.
